title: How changing HIV treatment affects sleep, mood, quality of life and health in people around or after the menopause and older adults living with HIV
official: Perimenopause and older adults treatment outcomes and lived experience
summary:
Background and study aims 
People with HIV are living much longer. In many countries, more than half of people with HIV are now 50 or older, and this number is still growing. As people get older, their bodies change. Some people have problems with sleep or mood or feel side-effects from medicines. Women going through or after the menopause can also have new difficulties like these.
HIV medicines are tested in clinical trials, and these trials have shown that a treatment called bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir (B/F/TAF; Biktarvy) works well and is safe. But the people in trials do not always match the people who use the medicine in real life. For example, fewer older people and fewer women are often included. Trials also do not always measure everyday things that matter, like sleep, mood, quality of life or how satisfied people feel with their treatment.
Doctors often use B/F/TAF for older adults because it can be gentler on the kidneys and bones. But we still need more real-world information about how it feels to take this treatment, especially for older people and for women around menopause.
The PEARL study will collect information from several hospitals. It will look at older adults and people going through or after the menopause. By combining medical information with people’s lived experiences, we can learn which treatments suit them best. The results will help clinics give more personalised HIV care.

Who can participate?
Adults with HIV who fall into one of two populations: 
a)	Adults who are 60 years of age or older
b)	Individuals assigned female sex at birth who are between the ages of 40 to 60

Participants must also fall into one of these two groups: 
i) Individuals receiving B/F/TAF or who have ever received B/F/TAF as HIV treatment. 
ii) Individuals switching HIV treatment to any treatment regimen. 

What does the study involve?
If individuals provide their consent to participate, the staff members at their HIV clinic will complete a questionnaire with data on their gender, age, date of HIV diagnosis, routine blood results, medical treatment, and illnesses. The data will be extracted from their medical records. Following this, 1-2 months and 6-8 months after their enrolment, they will collect data from their routine visits to the clinic, including laboratory data and weight, medical history and other medications, HIV treatment history, drug-related clinical event at each of these timepoints. 

The study will not test any drugs and will not interfere with any treatment the participants may receive at the clinic. Participants are consenting to allow the researchers to gather routinely collected information about them and their care.

Participants in group (ii) above, will be required to complete a questionnaire at three timepoints: the time of enrollment,  after 1-2, and after 6-8 months. The questionnaire will take a maximum of 30 minutes to complete. It can be completed online in the comfort of their own home or at the clinic. After the completion of each questionnaire, participants will be given a £20 shopping voucher as a thank you for their time and effort.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participation in the PEARL study does not include any additional risks , although some people may find completing questionnaires tiresome. While there are no immediate benefits , many people enjoy knowing that their input will further knowledge about different treatment choices, and hopefully improve HIV care in perimenopausal and older adults.

Where is the study run from?
The study is being run by the University of Sussex and taking place in different UK HIV clinics.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
May 2026 to July 2027. The first HIV clinic will start running the study in May 2026. Each HIV clinic will run the study for 1 year and each participant's involvement will last no more than 8 months. 

Who is funding the study?
The PEARL study has received funding from Gilead Sciences who are the manufacturers of Bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (B/F/TAF). 

Who is the main contact for the study?
Please contact the study manager Dr Kate Alford - K.Alford@bsms.ac.uk or the chief investigator Dr Fiona Cresswell - F.Cresswell@bsms.ac.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Adults with HIV-1 
2. The potential participant has the mental capacity, and is willing  to, provide informed consent to participate in the study.
3. The individual falls into one of the two populations of interest:
3.1. Adults who are 60 years of age or older
3.2. Individuals assigned female sex at birth who are between the ages of 40 to 60 years
4.The participants must belong to one of two cohorts:
4.1. Routine data cohort: The individual is already receiving B/F/TAF, or has received B/F/TAF any time in the past 
OR
4.2. PROMs prospective cohort: The individual will be switching HIV treatment to either B/F/TAF or to an alternative ART regimen
Exclusion criteria:
1. In the opinion of the research team, the individual is unable or will be unwilling to comply with the study requirements
2. The individual has not provided informed consent
3. Data completeness is inadequate in the eyes of the site principal investigator
